title: Meninges & CSF Anatomy: Dura, Ventricles & Sinus Drains
description: Study meninges and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) anatomy, tracing the dura, arachnoid, and pia mater with choroid plexuses, ventricles, and dural venous sinus.
h1: Meninges, Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Ventricles and Dural Venous Sinuses
blurb: Three protective meningeal membranes (dura, arachnoid, pia), buoyancy-providing cerebrospinal fluid from choroid plexuses, and dural venous sinus drainage.
lead: Suspended in crystal-clear cerebrospinal fluid and wrapped in three protective membranes, the living brain floats inside the skull so its own weight does not crush its base. In this illustrated guide to meninges and cerebrospinal fluid, we examine 20 documented structures—including periosteal cranial dura, meningeal cranial dura, falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Suspended in crystal-clear cerebrospinal fluid and wrapped in three protective membranes, the living brain floats inside the skull so its own weight does not crush its base. Cranial dura has periosteal and meningeal layers that separate at dural venous sinuses and create falx/tentorium folds. The arachnoid bridges across sulci; CSF occupies the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia, which closely follows brain contours. Choroid plexus secretes much CSF into ventricles: lateral → interventricular foramina → third → cerebral aqueduct → fourth → median/lateral apertures → subarachnoid cisterns. Arachnoid granulations drain much of it to dural sinuses, alongside other clearance routes. The subdural space is a potential pathologic space, not the normal CSF compartment. Within the human body, the meninges, csf & venous sinuses (Meninges · liquor cerebrospinalis · sinus durae matris) is situated in skull and spinal canal: layered coverings, ventricular cavities and dural venous channels, receives arterial perfusion via middle meningeal artery supplies dura; venous sinuses drain cerebral veins to jugular system, and is innervated by trigeminal and upper cervical sensory innervation to cranial dura; brain parenchyma itself lacks pain receptors.

The periosteal cranial dura (Stratum periostale durae) is outer cranial dural layer adherent to inner skull. Physiologically, the periosteal cranial dura forms tough outer covering and part of sinus walls. The meningeal cranial dura (Stratum meningeale durae) is inner tough dural layer reflecting as falx and tentorium. Physiologically, the meningeal cranial dura governs partitions cranial cavity and surrounds sinuses. Structurally, the falx cerebri comprises vertical sickle-shaped dural sheet between hemispheres. Physiologically, the falx cerebri supports superior and inferior sagittal sinuses. Structurally, the tentorium cerebelli comprises dural roof over cerebellum with tentorial notch around midbrain. Physiologically, the tentorium cerebelli governs partitions supratentorial and infratentorial spaces. Structurally, the superior sagittal sinus (Sinus sagittalis superior) comprises midline dural channel at upper attached edge of falx. Physiologically, the superior sagittal sinus receives superficial cerebral veins and arachnoid granulation drainage. Structurally, the straight sinus (Sinus rectus) comprises sinus at falx–tentorium junction receiving inferior sagittal and great cerebral venous drainage. Physiologically, the straight sinus governs transfers deep cerebral venous return posteriorly.

Clinically, regarding the periosteal cranial dura, spinal epidural space differs from cranial periosteal interface. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the meningeal cranial dura, dural folds constrain mass displacement. In clinical pathology involving the falx cerebri, bridging veins cross toward its superior sinus. Medical evaluation of the tentorium cerebelli also notes that herniation at notch threatens brainstem.

questions.question: What are the three meninges around the brain?
questions.answer: From outside inward they are dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater. Cerebrospinal fluid occupies the subarachnoid space. The arachnoid mater (Arachnoidea mater) is thin membrane deep to dura spanning over sulci; trabeculae bridge to pia. Physiologically, the arachnoid mater governs bounds CSF-filled subarachnoid space.

questions.question: Where does cerebrospinal fluid flow?
questions.answer: CSF circulates through the ventricles and subarachnoid spaces before being returned to venous or lymphatic drainage pathways. Structurally, the choroid plexus (Plexus choroideus) comprises vascular core with specialized epithelial covering in ventricles. Physiologically, the choroid plexus secretes much of cerebrospinal fluid and forms blood–CSF barrier.

questions.question: What is the periosteal cranial dura?
questions.answer: Outer cranial dural layer adherent to inner skull. Functionally, it forms tough outer covering and part of sinus walls. In clinical pathology involving the periosteal cranial dura, spinal epidural space differs from cranial periosteal interface.

questions.question: Where is the falx cerebri located?
questions.answer: Vertical sickle-shaped dural sheet between hemispheres. Functionally, it supports superior and inferior sagittal sinuses. Medical evaluation of the falx cerebri also notes that bridging veins cross toward its superior sinus.

questions.question: What is the function of the superior sagittal sinus?
questions.answer: Functionally, it receives superficial cerebral veins and arachnoid granulation drainage. Midline dural channel at upper attached edge of falx. Clinically, regarding the superior sagittal sinus, sinus thrombosis impairs venous outflow.
